summary: Jeff Yass on economic myths: US debt should be measured against wealth not GDP, consumer surplus and entrepreneurs, tax myths and school vouchers. Policy-opinion discussion, little trading content. Main points: US wealth about $230T makes debt manageable; the risk is destroying the growth engine.

coverage.note: US debt versus wealth rather than GDP; waste; risk is wealth destruction
regulation and taxes kill growth; consumer surplus and entrepreneurs capture 10%
vilifying the rich; zero-sum myth, consumer surplus examples
taxes on billionaires myth; Buffett philanthropy
school choice vouchers, hidden government cost, expected value of ideas
welfare by vouchers; closing; nothing else

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: So our real wealth is so enormous that the debt really isn't a problem.
claims.claim: US debt should be judged against national wealth (about $230 trillion, roughly 7x GDP, with a stock market of $80 trillion, over 2.5x GDP, unlike Europe or China at about 1x) rather than against GDP; on that basis debt is only about 13-14% of wealth, a historic low, even though debt/GDP is near 100%.
claims.indicator: debt to national wealth vs debt to GDP; stock market cap / GDP
claims.conditions: Debt-to-GDP was a good proxy for a long time, no longer because US wealth is so large; he says it is a historic low on wealth
claims.testable: yes - ratios computable from Fed financial accounts and market cap data

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: The way we go broke is if that $230 trillion wealth gets annihilated
claims.claim: The real risk to US solvency is a collapse in wealth (e.g. from $230 trillion to $100 trillion, where it was 10-15 years ago) caused by bad policy; as long as the growth engine of business creation continues there is no need to worry about debt.
claims.indicator: US national wealth / stock market value
claims.conditions: Bad policy that destroys business formation and wealth
claims.testable: partly - wealth collapse scenario, depends on policy

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: we're spending 7 trillion when 5 trillion could have gotten the same job done.
claims.claim: Federal spending is wasteful by about $2 trillion a year (spending $7 trillion where $5 trillion would do), which is a shame but not a solvency threat.
claims.testable: no - the waste estimate is an assertion

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: we're roughly the same, you know, population as as most of Europe, and we're 50% richer.
claims.claim: Regulation that blocks business start-ups and very high taxes that stop capital raising would sharply cut growth; the US is 50% richer than Europe with similar population, so modest policy changes could make it much poorer.
claims.indicator: regulation and tax burden vs business formation
claims.conditions: He mentions this may be seen in 2029

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: I say the typical number somewhere around 10%.
claims.claim: Entrepreneurs capture only about 10% of the value they create (Bezos about 2% of Amazon's value once consumer surplus of $10 trillion is counted) and the rest goes to consumers as consumer surplus.
claims.indicator: consumer surplus (time saved x multiple of 20)
claims.conditions: Estimates use time saved valued at a 20x multiple
claims.testable: partly - consumer surplus is hard to measure

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: to have a tax system and a culture that vilifies these people is absolutely upside down.
claims.claim: Because most benefit goes to consumers, taxing and vilifying entrepreneurs is counterproductive; the zero-sum 'one big pizza pie' view of wealth is a misconception.

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: building up a huge tax liability in the future as his stock goes up
claims.claim: Billionaires do pay tax: the company pays corporate tax on shareholders' behalf (20% of $30 billion is $6 billion for Bezos), and unrealised gains build a future tax liability, so claims that they pay zero are factually wrong.

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: the example I often give is $43,000 per kid in New York City.
claims.claim: School vouchers would give education at about half the price, since New York spends $43,000 per pupil while the best Catholic schools cost less than half; competition would improve results and reduce waste and fraud.
claims.testable: partly - cost and outcome comparisons exist

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: they don't send you a bill uh for school.
claims.claim: Government hides costs by not billing citizens directly, so waste persists; if people saw the bill, they would change their behaviour.

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: it's also idea times the probability that it's actually doable.
claims.claim: In choosing causes, the value is the size of the benefit times the probability it can be achieved, so a smaller idea with high chance beats a bigger one with near zero chance.

claims.speaker: Jeff Yass
claims.quote: I would say voucher, voucher, voucher.
claims.claim: Welfare should be delivered by vouchers (as food stamps) for schools and health care instead of government-run systems, a far more efficient welfare state.
